The post Review: Tequila El Mexicano Anejo appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Tequila El Mexicano, part of Foley Family Wines & Spirits, has finally launched its first anejo. We’ve never covered any of the offerings from the brand, but we’re starting here, with this release that was rested for 14 to 16 months in American and French oak. Agaves are aged a minimum of 6 years and are grown in the Jalisco Highlands. The Master Tequilero behind the brand is Don Félix Bañuelos, who previously cofounded Tequila Cazadores.

Some more distillation details: “The family uses a careful two-stage ‘low and slow’ cooking method in stainless steel autoclaves for up to 24 hours. Their unique seven-day open-air fermentation – one of the longest in modern tequila production – is enhanced by classical music, stimulating the natural yeast growth. While most distilleries employ copper stills, León Sr. designed stainless steel pot stills to double distill El Mexicano, preserving the agave’s true flavor.”

Tequila El Mexicano Anejo Review

The short of it is that this is an extremely soft tequila, something I’d probably chalk up to the use of French oak in the aging process. Any peppery agave notes on the nose are immediately tempered, showing more cinnamon and nutmeg, well-doused in brown butter. A vague note of chocolate and some coffee elements ring the edges of the experience, giving the experience something of a Sunday pastry vibe.

The palate follows suit, almost to a T. Soft and infused with baking spice, the tequila feels like a caramel glaze intended to be drizzled over a flan or a gingery cake, only less overtly sweet. There’s plenty of sugar in the mix, but it’s tempered with ground coffee, bittersweet cocoa powder, and a light skin of barrel char. An element of brown banana becomes prominent as the finish builds, with a reprise of spice roaring back into the picture as the experience concludes. Curiously, the fade-out is a bit gravelly and earthy, which helps further to temper the up-front sweetness but which doesn’t entirely play to the tequila’s biggest strengths.

80 proof. NOM 1588.

B / $50 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Rosebank 32 Years Old

The post Review: Rosebank 32 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Once called “The King of the Lowlands,” Scotland’s Rosebank Distillery was founded in 1840, shuttered in 1993, and refurbished around 2020. Since then, new owners Ian Macleod Distillers have dripped out rare offerings from pre-closure casks, starting with a well-received 30 year old single malt. We previously covered the (fantastic) 31 year old, bottled in 2022.

And now, Rosebank’s “Legacy Series” rounds out its trilogy with a 32 year old, once again blended from an undisclosed but undoubtedly small parcel of vintage barrels. It was actually bottled back in 2023, but the whisky is just now being made available in the American market. (In highly limited quantities, of course.)

Back then, the whisky was produced nearly identically to how the new-look Rosebank makes it today: triple distillation with worm tub condensers, a combo unique in Scotch production. So how did more than three decades in cask treat this particular offering?

Let’s find out.

Rosebank 32 Years Old Review

The nose kicks off just a tiny bit chemical at first, as if the early vapors were the last vestiges of some bygone cleaning solution. And then, suddenly, it blossoms. Elegant honeyed sweetness, almond extract, and light touch of cinnamon-infused simple syrup highlight aromas remarkably delicate for 32 years in cask. Fruit builds and eventually coalesces with confectionary notes — in time, this ends up smelling a lot like Taiwanese pineapple cakes, crossed with lemon meringue pie. Some green and vegetal notes lie even further in, but they’re almost afterthoughts, like a sprig of mint atop a fruit tart.

The first time I sampled Rosebank 32, I was lucky to do so alongside a pour of Rosebank 31. Comparison may be the thief of joy, but this particular side-by-side left me pretty happy. Next to its predecessor, the 32 starts off perhaps a touch creamier. It’s also slightly more herbal and even lightly savory, at least early on; here, fried sage meets a little sweet & sour sauce. But things change once again at the midpalate, moving toward burnt citrus peel and tropical fruit, the latter opening up into overripe pineapple, papaya, and guava.

Toasted oak and allspice carry us through to the back palate before a long and mildly tannic finish. At the very end, nut extracts and malt take back the reins. It’s effectively a final shift back from cask to distillate.

Inviting, accessible, and never boring, this is easily another feather in Rosebank’s cap. The deeper you dig, the more you’ll find.

95.2 proof.

A / $2000 (700ml)

title: Review: Redemption Straight Bourbon (2026)
summary:
The many acts of the Redemption whiskey brand continue to evolve. This year, Redemption not only introduced new bottles and packaging (spurred by a trademark infringement lawsuit from Bulleit over the look of its old bottles; Bulleit won but no money changed hands), it reformulated its bourbon, upping the abv from 42% to 46%. With…

The post Review: Redemption Straight Bourbon (2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
The many acts of the Redemption whiskey brand continue to evolve. This year, Redemption not only introduced new bottles and packaging (spurred by a trademark infringement lawsuit from Bulleit over the look of its old bottles; Bulleit won but no money changed hands), it reformulated its bourbon, upping the abv from 42% to 46%.

With Master Blender Alan Kennedy at the helm, the source juice is the same — MGP spirit with a 75% corn, 21% rye, 4% barley mashbill (stamped right on the front label!) — but it’s bottled at a noticeably higher proof. The new bottle is more modern and, to my eye, appealing, “featuring an eagle in mid-flight, formed from rye with its wings spread wide,” embossed in the glass.

“Setbacks aren’t the end of the story. They’re often the beginning of something stronger,” said Mike Dee, President of [brand owner] Deutsch Family Wine & Spirits. “The team embraced the moment as an opportunity to elevate both the package and the bourbon, which we believe will propel distribution and volume to new heights. The overwhelmingly positive reaction from our distributor partners thus far validates Redemption’s new stature and brand proposition in both on and off-premise environments.”

Redemption’s Rye and High Rye Bourbon both also received refreshed packaging but were already at 92 proof, so nothing has changed on those, recipe-wise. Note that batch numbers are no longer indicated on the label.

Redemption Straight Bourbon (2026) Review

There’s still no age statement on Redemption, but the price point remains an indicator that this is still very young stuff. While it’s not the “high rye” offering, the grassy pop of fresh rye makes an aromatic impact, tempering what is otherwise a fairly corn-forward nose with elements of ginger and clove. The latter is more prominent now than in previous expressions (see our reviews of the 2020 and 2016 releases), thanks surely to the higher alcohol level, but the overall presentation is fairly mainstream, arguably anonymous.

The palate is quite corn-heavy, with lots of peanut giving the whiskey a Cracker Jack quality that clings to you. Vanilla and butterscotch notes take their time to wander into view, the body becoming oddly malty as it develops. Surprisingly, the higher abv makes less of an impact on the tongue than it does on the racier nose. Youth, I suppose, will do that to a whiskey. The finish is rather doughy, almost chewy, with gentler overtones of almond paste, light on the sugar.

As I’ve said before: It’s harmless, but best for punch.

92 proof.

B / $30 [BUY IT NOW FROM TOTAL WINE] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Cedar Ridge Anniversary Edition Bourbon 2026
summary:
In 2025, Iowa’s Cedar Ridge Distillery celebrated 20 years of operations with its first Anniversary Edition Bourbon, which finished its standard bourbon in a wide array of secondary casks. (Cedar Ridge is also an operational winery, and many of its casks are sourced in house.) According to Master Blender Murphy Quint, it was the most…

The post Review: Cedar Ridge Anniversary Edition Bourbon 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
In 2025, Iowa’s Cedar Ridge Distillery celebrated 20 years of operations with its first Anniversary Edition Bourbon, which finished its standard bourbon in a wide array of secondary casks. (Cedar Ridge is also an operational winery, and many of its casks are sourced in house.) According to Master Blender Murphy Quint, it was the most popular whiskey in the distillery’s history. Naturally, Quint and his team decided to make Anniversary Edition an annual release.

For the 2026 version, Quint started with some of his mature Iowa bourbon, made from 74% corn, 14% rye, and 12% malted barley. The whiskey then went into five different finishing casks, which previously held Madeira, Napa Cabernet, Pedro Ximenez sherry, Tawny Port, and Tokaji.

“I wanted to keep a similar foundation to last year’s release with sherry and Tokaji finishes, but I chose PX sherry to work with instead of my usual Amontillado,” says Quint. “The Madeira and Napa Cabernet casks are what really push this blend in a new direction.”

The final blend was bottled at 112 proof. Let’s see how it tastes.

Cedar Ridge Anniversary Edition Bourbon 2026 Review

The base spirit is bourbon, but those finishing casks certainly lead the charge on the nose. Jammy dark fruits immediately pop, followed by cinnamon, and then eventually a dried fruit medley: sultanas, apricots, and pear slices. Oxidized wine settles in and dominates from here on out, with components including roasted chestnuts, toasted walnuts, and nearly burnt toffee. Leathery tannins also sit deeply in the nostrils; on the flip side, there’s some familiar bourbon vanilla and caramel hiding in there as well, begging to be picked up just below the surface. Those back-end elements lend a sort of à la mode quality, and suddenly, you’ve got dark fruit compote spooned atop a scoop of ice cream. Murphy Quint certainly threw a lot at the underlying bourbon, but he didn’t entirely bury it.

There’s no hiding that Napa Cab on the first sip, and as far as fruit goes, early tastes include hefty dark cherry and cinnamon sticks. Blackcurrant and boysenberry jams lend a surprising amount of tartness. A big transition occurs right before the midpalate, as flavors shift much sweeter toward rich pan caramel, vanilla glaze, and treacle. A consistent narrative forms across sips, each moving from bold, tangy fruit to boldly sweet, then finally to peppery spice. (Flavors are boisterous throughout, and the whiskey clearly has no interest in stopping if the drinker falls behind.) At the back palate, more black cherry syrup meets baking spice. Finally — and thankfully — some recognizable bourbon peeks through on the finish. In true Cedar Ridge fashion, it’s a touch crafty, slightly grainy, and very peppery. I almost wish it had come through sooner.

To me, this is a step up on last year’s inaugural Anniversary Edition, though perhaps a rung below the distillery’s absolute best stuff. It’s tasty, but it never quite achieves beautiful harmony between whiskey and multiple cask finishes. (For such a hit, the QuintEssential American Single Malt immediately springs to mind.)

112 proof.

B+ / $65

title: Review: Holiday Vodka
summary:
Holiday Vodka was “born from a feeling,” but more to the point it’s made in Italy, using 100% soft Italian wheat from Piedmont and water from Fonti Bauda, 1080 meters above sea level in the Maritime Alps. Distillation takes place at La Canellese, also located in Piedmont. The bottle, to me at least, alternately evokes…

The post Review: Holiday Vodka appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Holiday Vodka was “born from a feeling,” but more to the point it’s made in Italy, using 100% soft Italian wheat from Piedmont and water from Fonti Bauda, 1080 meters above sea level in the Maritime Alps. Distillation takes place at La Canellese, also located in Piedmont. The bottle, to me at least, alternately evokes a flower vase and an upturned zeppelin.

Holiday Vodka Review

Wheat-based vodkas can often land on the sweet side, and Holiday is no exception. In fact, it’s notably sweet, to the point where it’s one of the spirit’s most defining features.

The nose hints at that trait, though it’s not overwhelming or overt, although the aroma remains focused on notes of ripe, almost mushy banana, with a vanilla kick. A light industrial quality is detectable beneath the aromas of banana cream pie, but the sweeter elements soon intensify in the glass to the point where it quickly fades into the ether.

On the palate, sugar is immediate and intense. Bananas in cream remain the dominant flavor, with ample vanilla and caramel layered over all of it. There’s no hint of booziness or industrial elements here, and the sweetness never fades even on the lasting finish, which feels like a liquified version of a vanilla wafer.

Holiday’s website shows photos of this vodka used in a martini, which seems downright insane to me. Cosmo, yes. Martini, no.

80 proof.

B / $26

title: Review: Silverthorn Reserve Finisher’s Art Port Finish Whiskey 10 Years Old and Blender’s Art Rye 10 Years Old
summary:
Some art looks like an accident. A Jackson Pollock painting can appear to be little more than paint thrown across a canvas. A jazz improvisation can sound as if the musician is making decisions in real time with no plan beyond the next note. A sculpture can look as though its creator simply stopped working…

The post Review: Silverthorn Reserve Finisher’s Art Port Finish Whiskey 10 Years Old and Blender’s Art Rye 10 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Some art looks like an accident.

A Jackson Pollock painting can appear to be little more than paint thrown across a canvas. A jazz improvisation can sound as if the musician is making decisions in real time with no plan beyond the next note. A sculpture can look as though its creator simply stopped working at the precise moment the rest of us would have kept going.

But art rarely happens by accident.

Behind the finished work are choices. Thousands of them, sometimes. What to add. What to remove. What to combine. What to leave alone. Where to stop. The viewer may never know those decisions were made, but they are there all the same.

Whiskey can work much the same way.

It is easy to look at a blend and think, “So they put a bunch of barrels together.” It is just as easy to look at a finished whiskey and think, “So they put it in another barrel for a while.” Technically, those descriptions aren’t wrong. But they tell us almost nothing about what went into making the whiskey we ultimately find in the bottle.

Which barrels were selected? Why those barrels? In what proportions? What was the blender trying to achieve? What did one whiskey contribute that another could not? When is a secondary cask doing what the whiskey needs, and when is it simply doing something because it can? How many possible decisions sit between an individual barrel and the whiskey that eventually reaches a bottle?

There are countless ways to answer those questions, and the answers can make one whiskey very different from another.

After more than a decade as CEO of Sagamore Spirit in Baltimore, Drew Thorn launched Silverthorn Reserve in 2025. The brand releases single barrel expressions, but its primary focus is on something Thorn considers more artistic: creating highly individual blends and finishes rather than relying solely on what a single barrel happens to offer.

That approach puts the decisions behind the whiskey at the forefront. Blenders can take very different approaches to combining barrels. Finishing whiskey, or giving it a secondary maturation, can be handled in many different ways. The choice of barrels, proportions, timing and countless other variables can take a whiskey in a particular direction, separating the final product from every other bottle sitting on the shelf.

The artistry, in other words, may be hiding in plain sight.

Drew Thorn sent Drinkhacker Batch 1 of Silverthorn Reserve Blender’s Art Rye 10 Years Old and Batch 1 of Silverthorn Reserve Finisher’s Art Port Finish Whiskey 10 Years Old for review. Both are opportunities to look past the bottle and consider the decisions that went into making what is inside it.

So, let’s take a closer look at Thorn’s work as an artist.

And then there is the question every artist eventually has to face: Is the finished work worthy of a place in a museum?

Silverthorn Reserve Blender’s Art: The Rye Blend 10 Years Old (Batch 1) Review

Batch 1 is a blend of eight barrels of rye whiskey distilled by MGP in Lawrenceburg, Indiana.

Thirty-seven percent of the blend comes from a mashbill of 51% rye, 44% corn, and 5% malted barley. Those barrels were aged between 10 years 4 months and 10 years 8 months, with the final 1.5 years spent aging in Baltimore, Maryland.

The remainder of the blend is made up of 95% rye and 5% malted barley. Even within that portion, there is plenty of variation. Twelve percent of the total blend consists of 95/5 rye aged for 13 years 7 months. That barrel was filled on February 5, 2013, spending the first half of its life in Indiana and most of the second half of maturation in Templeton, Iowa.

Another 36% of the total blend is 95/5 rye barreled on November 9, 2015, which spent almost all of its 10 years and 9 months of maturation in Indiana.

The final 15% is what makes this release especially interesting. It is also 10.5-year-old 95/5 rye, initially entered into a Kelvin barrel with a #3 char on November 9, 2015. After two years in that first barrel, the rye was transferred to a new Kelvin barrel with a #3 char for another eight years.

The natural harvest proof of the blend was 114 proof.

On the nose, the whiskey shows the bright profile commonly associated with MGP-distilled rye, along with more oak presence than has been typical of MGP rye in recent years. Dry apple cider leads, followed quickly by the bread and spice of coffee cake. As the bready cinnamon note gives way, tea tree oil becomes quite prominent, with peanut brittle providing sweetness and an earthy counterpoint.

Despite being somewhat younger, the nose is more nuanced than several 13-year-old MGP ryes currently on the market.

That brightness continues on the palate, where peppermint candy meets candied ginger, creating a cooling sensation that persists throughout the tasting. Nilla Wafers and Bit-O-Honey appear through the mid-palate, but the spicy cooling quality never quits.

On the finish, the candied ginger turns toward ginger beer, while the peppermint takes on the character of eucalyptus cough drops. The cooling sensation continues, followed by a late push of cinnamon that adds another push of spice.

For anyone who enjoys the big, bright ryes distilled in Indiana, this is a beauty. The nose suggests more oak than the palate ultimately delivers, with the palate placing greater emphasis on the whiskey’s brightness while avoiding the rough edges that can accompany younger Indiana rye.

Drew Thorn’s experience blending these two mashbills is evident throughout the whiskey. 113 proof. A- / $100

Silverthorn Reserve Finisher’s Art Port Finish Whiskey (Batch 1) Review

Batch 1 is a blend of six rye whiskey barrels distilled by MGP in Lawrenceburg, Indiana. Fifty-seven percent of the blend comes from a mashbill of 95% rye and 5% malted barley, with those barrels filled on August 20, 2015 and aged for 10 years and one month. The remaining 43% comes from a mashbill of 51% rye, 44% corn, and 5% malted barley, with those barrels filled on December 22, 2014 and aged for 10 years and eight months.

As the six barrels were marrying together in a tank, the original casks were seasoned with one gallon of 10-year-old Tawny Port, which sells for $35 per bottle. Thorn developed a custom apparatus for conditioning the barrels, consisting of a stainless-steel rod fitted with an atomizing and aerating tip that was inserted through the barrel bung. The Tawny Port was atomized into a fine mist inside the barrel, after which the barrel was sealed and brought to approximately 6 to 7 psi of CO2 pressure. That pressure forced the Tawny Port mist into the oak over a period of one to two hours.

The rye whiskey blend was then entered into the Port-seasoned original casks at 104 proof on September 10, 2025. After 54 days of secondary maturation, the barrels were dumped for blending on November 11, 2025, yielding a natural harvest proof of 101.

The nose opens with clove and a light touch of cedar that stays well short of overpowering. Prune juice brings the Tawny Port forward early, while sarsaparilla arrives later with considerable push. It makes for one of the more enjoyable rye whiskey noses I’ve encountered in quite some time.

On the palate, the rye remains firmly at the forefront without being overshadowed by the Tawny Port. Dill and cream soda appear early, followed by dark chocolate and blackberry bramble through the mid-palate. The mouthfeel is medium in viscosity.

The finish brings lesser-sweetened raisins, basil, and a touch of wintergreen. The final note is a throwback to chewing on a No. 2 pencil, bringing back a very specific elementary-school memory.

I absolutely love this finished rye. The Tawny Port influence is plainly evident, yet it never takes over the whiskey. There is a real sense of minimalism in how the finishing component has been applied, making this a textbook example of “less is more.” 100 proof. A / $100

title: Review: SunnyD Vodka Seltzer Purple
summary:

Bet you didn’t know there’s another version of it, too — one that trades orange for purple. SunnyD Vodka Seltzer Purple is, exactly as the name suggests, a seltzified version of purple drink, purportedly…

The post Review: SunnyD Vodka Seltzer Purple appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Bet you didn’t know there’s a boozy version of the decadent delight — er, delite — you loved as a kid, SunnyD!

Bet you didn’t know there’s another version of it, too — one that trades orange for purple.

SunnyD Vodka Seltzer Purple is, exactly as the name suggests, a seltzified version of purple drink, purportedly made with vodka, fruit juice, and — interestingly — no sugar. A 12 oz. can has only 95 calories — presuming you can finish the whole thing. I couldn’t.

I’ve had this sitting on my desk since it launched six months ago, unable to bring myself to crack it open until now. Part of my still wishes I hadn’t. The flavor is best described as a liquid nightmare: strong overtones of industrial chemicals, followed by sickly sweet grape candy and some kind of low-cal sweetener. (SunnyD says there are no artificial sweeteners, so I’m guessing this is made with stevia.)

Undrinkable yet vaguely nostalgic, it’s an experience that lingers for quite some time thanks to its monstrous and lasting finish. Not in a good way.

4.5% abv.

D- / $10 per four-pack of 12 oz cans

summary:
Angel’s Envy’s latest Distillery Series bottling — its third — carries a doozy of a name — and a finishing regimen. This straight bourbon leans on two finishing barrels, which seemingly couldn’t be further apart from one another: stout beer and exotic amburana wood. The stout finishing dominates: 99% of the whiskey in this batch…

The post Review: Angel’s Envy Bourbon Finished in Stout & Amburana Barrels appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Angel’s Envy’s latest Distillery Series bottling — its third — carries a doozy of a name — and a finishing regimen. This straight bourbon leans on two finishing barrels, which seemingly couldn’t be further apart from one another: stout beer and exotic amburana wood.

The stout finishing dominates: 99% of the whiskey in this batch was finished in Goose Island and Trellis Brewing stout barrels, including both first-fill (40%) and second-fill (60%) barrels, for up to two years.

Only 1% of the whiskey touches polarizing amburana wood, and even then it was only in amburana for a month.

You’ll need to head to Angel’s Envy‘s distillery in Louisville to pick up a bottle, and if you do, here’s what to expect.

Angel’s Envy Bourbon Finished in Stout & Amburana Barrels Review

This may have just the lightest kiss of amburana in production, but its evidence is decidedly outsized in the finished product. It’s most visible on the nose: sweet and maple syrupy, punctuated heavily with candy corn and caramel corn notes. Things get a bit more traditional from there, with notes of vanilla and some rustic barrel char in attendance, though the syrupy amburana never recedes far from view.

It’s tough to suss out exactly what a year or two in stout barrels has done to this whiskey, though the palate offers a few hints, at least. A dark chocolate character builds quickly, perhaps evoking stout, and is chased by vanilla, butterscotch, and, finally, more of that maple character, which lingers well into the finish. That’s amburana, it seems, roaring back into the limelight and giving the outro a real cake frosting quality that clings to you for the long haul. The rest of the experience? Buried in the dessert aisle.

I enjoyed this well enough, but I sure would love to see how it fared without the amburana at all. 100 proof. B+ / $55 (375ml)

title: Review: Firestone Walker Oktoberfest 2026
summary:

It’s fully brewed with German ingredients aside from…

The post Review: Firestone Walker Oktoberfest 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Break out the lederhosen and get the pretzels in the oven! October is here and it’s time to celebrate all things German.

This year’s brew is a collaboration between Firestone Walker and Mahrs Bräu, a brewery in Bamberg (originator of smoky rauchbier) that is 356 years old. It’s fully brewed with German ingredients aside from California water — including Bamberger Pilsen malt, Mahrs Bräu’s own malt, and Hallertau Tradition and Hersbrucker hops — a Festbier designed to emulate what drinking beer in October (really September) in Germany tastes like.

The results are, as expected, uncanny. It really tastes like an authentic German lager, quite malty and ever so lightly fruity with notes of baked apples and banana. Chewy with decidedly moderated bitterness, the gentle sweetness helps the beer feel light as a feather despite its healthy 6% abv. At the same time, the beer has plenty of fest-friendly gravity, offering a rounded, mouth-filling exuberance that ensures a delightful pairing with everything from schnitzel to spätzle and beyond — or just drinking on its own.

6% abv.

A- / $12 per 4-pack of 16 oz cans

title: Review: Smokeye Hill Barrel Proof Bourbon 5 Years Old
summary:
Last summer, we got our first taste of Smokeye Hill, the buzzy Colorado Springs-based whiskey brand notable for the use of heirloom blue corn in their whiskey recipes. David had a chance to review their impressive barrel proof rye whiskey in the fall, and now we’re finally getting to the third, and perhaps most talked…

The post Review: Smokeye Hill Barrel Proof Bourbon 5 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Last summer, we got our first taste of Smokeye Hill, the buzzy Colorado Springs-based whiskey brand notable for the use of heirloom blue corn in their whiskey recipes. David had a chance to review their impressive barrel proof rye whiskey in the fall, and now we’re finally getting to the third, and perhaps most talked about, whiskey in their lineup.

Like the standard bourbon, Smokeye Hill Barrel Proof is distilled on contract from a four-grain mashbill of yellow corn, rye, malted barley, and heirloom blue corn, a nod to the brand’s southwest origins that reportedly makes up more than 50% of the recipe. That spirit ages for at least five years in a mix of 30- and 53-gallon barrels with varying char levels from No. 2 to all the way up to No. 5, a full minute or more of charring that borders on incineration. While the base spirit remains unchanged in each cask, that unique barrel program presumably gives blenders a broader maturation profile to work with. Let’s see how it all works at full strength.

Smokeye Hill Barrel Proof Bourbon 5 Years Old Review

There’s quite a bit of ethanol at the outset here, and like the standard bourbon, some youthful notes come through initially. Grain-forward hints of warm cornbread and a little blue corn grist add a slightly savory edge to things but give way rather quickly to sweeter toffee, vanilla cream, and chewy caramel. At barrel strength, there’s more sweetness coming through than with the standard bourbon, but it’s dark and caramelized. With even more time in the glass, brown butter, pecan pralines, and caramel corn arrive.

The palate delivers barrel proof heft and heat right out of the gate, kicking off with chili pepper, freshly ground cinnamon, whole clove, and plenty of fresh oak and walnut shells. It’s a peppery warmth that goes straight to the nostrils before hugging the back of the throat. Once things settle down, caramel sauce, dark brown sugar, and dried orange peel fill the midpalate with a generous, silky sweetness. The finish kicks off with an unexpected zip of bright wintergreen and candied pineapple before eroding into an off-dry conclusion of pink peppercorn, oak, barrel char, and a little cigar wrapper. At cask proof, this bourbon demands some patience and comes across just a bit too hot in places. Still, it’s showing a lot of promise. Like the standard bourbon, it would likely do very well in a classic whiskey cocktail.
